newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: PLO urges U.N. measures to halt Israel settlements.
newsitem.headline: PLO urges U.N. measures to halt Israel settlements.

text.p: The Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) called on the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday to adopt "collective measures" against Israel, including blocking assistance to those building settlements in occupied territory.

The PLO's U.N. observer, Nasser al-Kidwa, was opening an emergency special session called for by Arab states seeking to halt Israel's construction of a housing project at a site in East Jerusalem captured in the 1967 Middle East war.

"There must be collective measures ... which will at least guarantee the prohibition of assistance to those who violate international law, preventing them from receiving finances and rewards," Kidwa said, outlining the terms of a resolution expected to be submitted later.

He also called for action to ensure Israel respected the Fourth Geneva Convention, which prohibits settlements in occupied territories, and said the United Nations and the secretary-general "should become engaged in observing the situation."
"All of this should lead to the immediate cessation of the construction in Jabal Abu Ghneim and of all other settlement activities." The area is called Har Homa in Hebrew.

He said Israel's policies and actions not only violated international law, council resolutions and Middle East accords but "also represent the practical abandonment of the peace process and a declaration of the resumption of occupation."

"The most dangerous of such actions has been the commencement of construction of a new colonial settlement in Jabal Abu Ghneim to the south of occupied East Jerusalem, intended to absorb approximately 25,000 new colonial settlers," Kidwa said.
Jerusalem was the crux of the question of Palestine and "the key to peace and to war in the region," he added.

The emergency special session, expected to last two days, is the 10th convened under a 1950 "uniting for peace" procedure enabling an issue considered a threat to peace to be transferred to the 185-member assembly if a veto prevents action by the 15-nation Security Council. There is no veto in the Assembly, whose decisions are not binding.

The United States used its veto on March 7 and again on March 21 to block council resolutions calling on Israel not to proceed with the new settlement. While critical of Israel's action, it said the United Nations was not the forum for dealing with issues that should be resolved between the two sides.
On March 13, a non-emergency session of the General Asembly voted 130 to two, with two abstentions, for a resolution calling on Israel to abandon its construction plan.

Israeli representative David Peleg said the building of a new neighbourhood in Jerusalem, and any other dispute between Israel and the Palestinians, "cannot be considered, by any stretch of the imagination, a 'threat to international peace and security.'"
He called the emergency special session a "relic of the Cold War era" that was particularly discordant in the context of the Middle East peace process.

The decision to build at Har Homa, "an area within the municipal boundaries of Jerusalem where 75 percent of the land is Jewish owned, does not violate in any way any of the agreements with the Palestinians," he said.
Pending the conclusion of negotiations on permanent status issues, the Palestinian Authority "does not have any standing in the city of Jerusalem," he added.
Peleg said the importance of every step taken by Israel in accordance with its commitments was minimised "while vociferous demands for further Israeli concessions were increased."

"Instead of continuing the negotiating process, the Palestinians embarked on a regional and international campaign to exert pressure and to isolate Israel if we did not accept all Palestinian positions," he said.
